newsitem.title: GERMANY: German banter offers glimpse of life under Euro bank.
newsitem.headline: German banter offers glimpse of life under Euro bank.

text.p: A deluge of confusing comments by council members of the German Bundesbank that have confounded markets may offer Europe a glimpse of life under the future European central bank once currency union is launched.

Economists said on Wednesday the decentralised struture of the future Euro central bank, which is modelled on the German central bank, means Europe may often be hit by market-roiling comments from policy makers such as Germany saw this week.

"We could very easily see increased market volatility once the European central bank comes into effect," said Holger Schmieding, an economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt. "There is going to be an awful lot of talking."

Although public debate about events in supranational bodies is nothing new, analysts said it is especially risky involving monetary policy, where even the slightest remark about interest rates can rattle global financial markets.
Analysts said the recent comments from top Bundesbank officials that often seemed to contradict one another painted a dire picture of how the public debate can unfold.

Several Bundesbank council members, each offering their own version of current German monetary policy, grabbed headlines at least 10 times over the last week, sometimes driving European markets higher and sometimes lower.

The problem lies in the structure of the future European central bank modelled after the Bundesbank, which was designed by the allied powers after World War Two to prevent a concentration of financial power in Germany, analysts said.

"It is almost to be feared that the European Central Bank will have the same kind of system" as the Bundesbank, said Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt about the bank, which will be based in Frankfurt.
"Public debate is almost inevitable with this kind of supranational institution," Grebe said.
According the Maastricht Treaty, the future European bank, which will supervise the single currency after its planned 1999 launch, will have an executive board made up of six people.
It will be roughly equivalent in function to the German central bank's directorate and conduct open market operations.

The European System of Central Banks (ESCB), made up of participating national central banks, will mirror the system of regional central bank presidents who make up the balance of the Bundesbank's decision-making council.
The strongest and most frequent statements are expected to come from the national central bank chiefs, as they do now from the German regional state central bank leaders, analysts said.

"These officials are going to be airing their differences in public," said Timo Klein, economist at MMS International in Frankfurt. "Once the ECB starts, there is going to be an active continuation of national interests."

Even more than the Bundesbank's regional central bank heads, ESCB representatives are widely expected to push views suited to economic events in their particular countries and are likely to feel obliged to publically argue for such policies.

"The European central bank will be even less disciplined than the Bundesbank," Merrill's Schmieding said. "Due to regional differences, they are going to be less coordinated than the Bundesbank has been."

Schmieding and others said the trick for central bank watchers and financial markets will be to quickly come to terms with which ESCB members reflect majority views on the policy-making council and those who have no power.
"The markets have a view of who is credible at the Bundesbank and it will take time to make the same sort of evaluations on the European central bank," said one analyst who asked not to be named.
